title: AGiR: Mitigating Gift Over-Reliance in Mixed-Motive Games
claim: Under the baseline mechanism an agent gets stuck in one sacrificial behavior; adding our plug-in lets it alternate and balance.
layout: 2 rows by 4 columns of frames, aligned to a central timeline arrow
description: The figure shows game-environment screenshots from a gridworld, arranged as two rows of four frames each. A horizontal timeline arrow runs through the middle, starting at a black dot labeled 'episode start' and continuing through four black time-step nodes. Dashed vertical arrows link each node to the frame above it and the frame below it. The top row is the baseline, where the disadvantaged agent is circled with a red dashed ring. It stays in the blue river or cleanup area in every frame. The bottom row uses the proposed method, where the agent is circled in green. It moves between the river and the apple-filled sand area. Frames show tan terrain, blue water, and red apple dots. Color-coded rings draw the eye first, and the contrast between red and green carries the comparison.
caption: We track the behavior of a disadvantaged agent under different gifting mechanisms. Top: LASE [ref]. A disadvantaged agent (red) is locked in cleanup (gift over-reliance). Bottom: LASE with AGiR (ours). A disadvantaged agent (green) escapes gift over-reliance by alternating between cleanup and harvest, leading to more balanced and sustainable behavior.
abstract: In this paper, we consider mixed-motive games (MMGs) which model various real-world multi-agent scenarios where self-interested agents must both cooperate and compete. We identify an issue with existing gifting methods, where agents become overly dependent on incoming gifts and fail to learn reward-yielding behaviors, a phenomenon we call gift over-reliance. To address this, we propose a refusal-augmented gifting framework that balances cooperation and competition in MMGs. Our approach introduces an adaptive refusal mechanism that allows agents to selectively reject a portion of received gifts from their policy-update signals, thereby mitigating gift over-reliance and preventing the agents from being exploited by other agents. This mechanism is gifting-method-agnostic, serving as a plug-in for existing schemes while enabling decentralized learning. We demonstrate that across diverse MMG environments and gifting schemes, our mechanism consistently reduces gift over-reliance and prevents lock-in to sacrificing policies, improving $Î±$-fairness as a result, without necessitating major changes to existing training pipelines.
